title: Evaluation of YouTube Videos as a Source of Information on Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing
screen_reason: Cross-sectional analysis of the 50 most-viewed English-language YouTube videos on non-invasive prenatal testing. Alongside the GQS, PEMAT and JAMA quality scales, two obstetricians made a separate factual-accuracy determination and report the share of the sample containing misinformation with its denominator (3/50 = 6%), the error being that the videos defined NIPT as a diagnostic rather than a screening test. That is explicit misinformation coding against clinical fact, so it is CONTENT, not QUALITY.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language YouTube search (authors based in Turkey)
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-viewed YouTube videos on non-invasive prenatal testing that contained misinformation
estimates.denominator: 50 English-language, relevant YouTube videos on non-invasive prenatal testing, the most-viewed results for the search term (60 screened; 4 non-English, 3 duplicates, 1 irrelevant and 2 from out-of-scope source types excluded)
estimates.definition: A video counted in the numerator if two obstetricians judged its content factually wrong; the Discussion states the error in all three cases was defining NIPT as a diagnostic test when it is a screening test.
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition; the paper's framing is that "Many websites contain incorrect, incomplete, biased, or misleading instructions, making it difficult for users to distinguish between reliable and false information", and the operational instance is a video "defining NIPT as a diagnostic test"

estimates.page_loc: p. 183, Results; restated on p. 184, Discussion ('in the present study 3 (6%) misleading videos were detected (defining NIPT as a diagnostic test)') and in the Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent obstetricians watched every video and applied a 9-item dichotomous content survey plus the GQS, PEMAT-A/V and JAMA Benchmark Criteria; 'in case of inconsistency, the videos were re-evaluated'. No kappa, percent agreement or written misinformation codebook is reported, and the misinformation judgement is not described as a separate instrument.

estimates.notes: The value itself is unambiguous and stated three times (abstract, results, discussion), but confidence is medium because the misinformation determination has no described procedure, no reliability statistic and no codebook — it appears as a single sentence in the results. denom_selection=curated: the frame is the top 50 videos sorted by view count, which the authors themselves flag as a limitation. Single-topic keyword corpus, so denom_scope=topical. One internal tension an adjudicator should see: the Methods say 'We evaluated one to two points from GQS scales as bad quality and misleading content', which would make 'misleading' a GQS band, yet the mean GQS was 2.96 overall and 1.42 for non-physician uploaders, so far more than 3 videos scored 1-2. The reported 6% therefore cannot be the GQS<=2 share; it is a separate factual-accuracy judgement, which is why it is coded CONTENT. The 6% is also strikingly low next to the same journal-literature the authors cite (they note prior YouTube studies found more health misinformation and attribute the gap to sample size), which is consistent with a top-50-by-views frame dominated by commercial and clinical uploaders.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) the 9 content-coverage questions in Table 4 (What is NIPT? 47/50 = 94%; How is NIPT done? 41 (82%); When? 37 (74%); What does it screen for? 36 (72%); How accurate? 29 (58%); Gender? 21 (42%); Should you get it? 17 (34%); Different kinds? 13 (26%); Limitations? 8 (16%)) — these are coverage/completeness shares, so a wholly accurate video can score low, which §3 puts on the QUALITY side; the 'insufficient data (84%) for limitations of the NIPT' figure in the Discussion is the complement of the 16% and would be a computed complement in any case. (2) GQS (mean 2.96 ± 0.62 overall; 4.5 ± 0.66 physicians vs 1.42 ± 0.57 non-physicians), PEMAT understandability 72% ± 16% and actionability 58% ± 28%, JAMA Benchmark 1.4 ± 0.8 — all reported as means only, and the rule is explicit that a scale reported only as a mean yields no row. Note the Methods define GQS 1-2 as 'bad quality and misleading content' but never report how many videos fell in that band, so no share is derivable. (3) Source composition (doctor/healthcare professional 38%, personal experience 34%, commercial/industry 28%; 62% of videos by non-doctors; 19 physician vs 31 non-physician uploaders) and 13 (26%) animated videos — producer and format descriptors, not veracity. (4) VPI 88.4 ± 14.2 and the view/like/dislike means. (5) The 6 (8.6%) misleading Sjogren's syndrome videos are quoted from Delli et al. and excluded under R8.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis. On 1 May 2021 the term 'Non-invasive prenatal testing' was entered in the YouTube search bar with the results sorted by view count; the first 50 most-viewed videos were analysed after excluding 4 non-English, 3 duplicated, 1 irrelevant and 2 out-of-scope-source videos from the 60 screened. No response rate applies. Two independent obstetricians watched every video and completed a 9-item dichotomous content survey derived from a published study of what people ask about NIPT, re-evaluating videos where they disagreed; quality was scored with GQS, PEMAT-A/V and the JAMA Benchmark Criteria, with mean values reported. No inter-rater reliability statistic is given anywhere, and the misinformation count is reported without a stated coding procedure. Authors' own limitations: single-day snapshot of a continuously changing platform, and restriction to the 50 most-viewed videos.
